e.meaning: perhaps hale and wide, from an old Germanic name
e.etymology: The English form of French Héloïse, of uncertain origin, perhaps from the Germanic name Helewidis, from heil, hale, and wid, wide. Known from the medieval lovers Abelard and Héloïse.

assoc.t: Eloise, the storybook girl who lives at the Plaza Hotel

e.etymology: From Old English Æthelthryth, from æthele, noble, and thryth, strength, by way of the medieval form Aldreda. Saint Audrey was a 7th-century queen who founded the abbey at Ely.
namesakes: Audrey Hepburn (actress, Breakfast at Tiffany's)
Audrey II (the man-eating plant in Little Shop of Horrors)

assoc.t: Audrey Hepburn, star of Breakfast at Tiffany's

e.etymology: From the English surname Ryder, an occupational name for a rider: a cavalryman, knight or mounted messenger. A modern arrival as a first name.
namesakes: Winona Ryder (actress, Stranger Things and Beetlejuice)

assoc.t: Ryder, truck rental and logistics company
Ryder, the boy who leads the PAW Patrol pups
Ryder Cup, US versus Europe golf tournament

e.meaning: misshapen head, or possibly helmeted head
e.etymology: From the Irish surname Ó Cinnéidigh, descendant of Cinnéidigh, a byname from ceann, head, and éidigh, ugly; some read it as helmeted head. Americans use it in honor of the Kennedy family.

assoc.t: President John F. Kennedy and his political family
Kennedy Space Center, NASA's Florida launch site

e.etymology: From an English surname, Emery plus -son; Emery goes back to Germanic names meaning brave ruler or home ruler. Often chosen in honor of essayist Ralph Waldo Emerson.
namesakes: Ralph Waldo Emerson (essayist and poet)

assoc.t: Ralph Waldo Emerson, essayist and poet (surname)
Emerson, electronics and appliance brand

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Old English heg, hay, plus denu, valley. In general use for girls as well as boys since the 1990s.
namesakes: Hayden Christensen (actor, Anakin Skywalker in Star Wars)
Hayden Panettiere (actress, Heroes and Nashville)

e.etymology: From Hebrew eder, flock, and El, God. In the Bible, Adriel is the nobleman who marries King Saul's daughter Merab.
From the English word for the season, which comes from Latin autumnus. Recorded as an American given name since the 1870s and widely used since the 1970s.

assoc.t: autumn, the season also called fall

e.etymology: Through French from Latin Vincentius, from vincens, conquering, a form of the verb vincere. Several early saints bore the name.
namesakes: Vincent van Gogh (Dutch painter)
Vincent Price (horror film actor)
Vincent Vega (John Travolta's hitman in Pulp Fiction)

assoc.t: Vincent, Don McLean's 1971 song about van Gogh

e.etymology: A modern American given name of unclear origin, in wide use since the 1990s, especially in Black families. It may build on Amar or Amare; the African and Hebrew meanings in name books are not well documented.
namesakes: Amari Cooper (NFL wide receiver)

e.etymology: From Greek iris, rainbow, and Iris, the goddess who personified it and carried messages for the gods. English speakers took it up with the flower names of the late 19th century.
namesakes: Iris West (love interest of The Flash)

assoc.t: iris, the garden flower
the iris, the colored part of the eye
Iris, the Goo Goo Dolls' 1998 hit ballad
Greek goddess of the rainbow

e.etymology: From the English surname for a bowman, from Anglo-Norman archer, ultimately Latin arcus, bow. A modern arrival as a first name.

assoc.t: Sterling Archer, spy of FX's animated comedy Archer

e.etymology: The English form of Irish Deaglán, Old Irish Declán, borne by Saint Declán of Ardmore, who founded a monastery in 5th-century Ireland. Its meaning is uncertain.
A northern English surname meaning son of Harry, the medieval English form of Henry.
namesakes: Harrison Ford (actor, Star Wars and Indiana Jones)
George Harrison (lead guitarist of the Beatles)
Benjamin Harrison (23rd US president)

e.etymology: From the legendary King Arthur. The name's origin is disputed: it may come from Welsh arth, bear, or from a Roman family name, Artorius.
namesakes: Arthur Ashe (tennis champion)
Arthur Miller (playwright, Death of a Salesman)
Arthur Conan Doyle (creator of Sherlock Holmes)

assoc.t: King Arthur, legendary ruler of Camelot
Arthur, PBS's cartoon aardvark

e.etymology: A Latinized form of Miles used in medieval England, of uncertain origin and often tied to Latin miles, soldier. In Slavic languages Milo is a short form of names built on mil, gracious or dear.
namesakes: Milo Ventimiglia (actor, This Is Us)
Milo (the boy hero of The Phantom Tollbooth)

assoc.t: The Adventures of Milo and Otis, 1989 pet film

e.etymology: From Arabic Aliya, the feminine of Ali, exalted or sublime. The spelling with a double A was popularized by the American R&B singer Aaliyah (1979-2001).

assoc.t: Aaliyah, R&B singer who died in a 2001 plane crash

e.etymology: The Italian form of John, from Latin Iohannes and Greek Ioannes, from Hebrew Yochanan, Yahweh is gracious.
namesakes: Giovanni Ribisi (actor, Friends and Avatar)

assoc.t: Don Giovanni, Mozart's opera about Don Juan
Giovanni, Team Rocket's boss in Pokémon

e.etymology: From Irish Conchúr, earlier Conchobhar, Old Irish Conchobar, lover of hounds. Conchobar mac Nessa is the king of Ulster in Irish legend.
namesakes: Connor McDavid (NHL star)
John Connor (humanity's future leader in the Terminator films)

e.meaning: from Brooklyn; originally Dutch for marshland
e.etymology: From the New York City borough, named for the Dutch town of Breukelen, from broek, marshland. As a girls' name it is also heard as Brook plus the -lyn ending.
namesakes: Brooklyn Beckham (son of David and Victoria Beckham)
Brooklyn Decker (model and actress)

assoc.t: Brooklyn, the New York City borough
Brooklyn Nets, NBA team
Brooklyn Nine-Nine, police sitcom

e.etymology: From the Latin saints' names Vivianus and Viviana, probably from vivus, alive. It has been both a man's and a woman's name in England; in the US it is almost entirely feminine.
namesakes: Vivian Vance (Ethel on I Love Lucy)
Vivian Ward (Julia Roberts's character in Pretty Woman)
Vivian Banks (Aunt Viv on The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air)

e.etymology: The English form of Caspar, the name medieval tradition gave to one of the three Magi, from an old Iranian word for treasurer. It is unrelated to the gemstone jasper, though the two sound alike.
namesakes: Jasper Johns (painter known for his American flags)
Jasper Hale (vampire in Twilight)

assoc.t: jasper, an opaque gemstone, usually red or brown
Jasper National Park in the Canadian Rockies

e.etymology: From Latin clara, the feminine of clarus, bright, clear or famous. Saint Clare of Assisi, a 13th-century follower of Saint Francis, made the name famous.
namesakes: Clara Barton (founder of the American Red Cross)
Clara (the girl in The Nutcracker ballet)
Clara Bow (silent film star)

assoc.t: Clara, the girl in The Nutcracker ballet

e.etymology: From the green ornamental stone, in general use as a name since the 1970s. The word comes from Spanish piedra de ijada, stone of the flank, because jade was thought to cure kidney pain.

assoc.t: jade, the green gemstone and its color

e.meaning: from Laurentum, an ancient town near Rome
e.etymology: The Italian and Spanish form of Laurence, from Latin Laurentius, man from Laurentum, a town near Rome whose name was linked with the laurel tree.
namesakes: Lorenzo de' Medici (Renaissance ruler of Florence)
Lorenzo Lamas (actor, Renegade)

e.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century from French Caroline, from Latin Carolina, the feminine of Carolus (Charles), which goes back to Germanic karl, free man.
namesakes: Caroline Kennedy (diplomat, daughter of John F. Kennedy)
Caroline Ingalls (Ma in Little House on the Prairie)

assoc.t: Sweet Caroline, Neil Diamond's sing-along hit

e.meaning: uncertain; perhaps beloved, bitter, or wished-for child
e.etymology: The Latin form of Mary, from Greek Maria and Hebrew Miryam, a name of debated meaning. As the name of the mother of Jesus it became the most widely used women's name in the Christian world.
namesakes: Maria von Trapp (the governess of The Sound of Music)
Maria Sharapova (tennis champion)
Maria Montessori (educator who founded Montessori schools)

assoc.t: the Virgin Mary, called Maria in most languages
Maria, the love song from West Side Story
Ave Maria, the Catholic prayer and its musical settings
Hurricane Maria, which devastated Puerto Rico in 2017

e.meaning: rival (from the Roman family name Aemilius)
e.etymology: The Spanish and Italian form of Latin Aemilianus, a derivative of the Roman family name Aemilius, traditionally linked to aemulus, rival. Its best-known bearer is Mexican revolutionary Emiliano Zapata.
namesakes: Emiliano Zapata (leader of the Mexican Revolution)

assoc.t: Emiliano Zapata, Mexican revolutionary

e.etymology: A Latinate form of Lilian used in Italian, Spanish and Polish, going back to Latin lilium, lily.

e.meaning: halo of light around the moon
e.etymology: A common Turkish name from ayla, the halo around the moon (ay). English speakers met it through Ayla, heroine of Jean Auel's 1980 novel The Clan of the Cave Bear. A separate Hebrew name Ayla means oak tree.

assoc.t: Ayla, heroine of The Clan of the Cave Bear

e.etymology: From Hebrew Yonah, dove. The biblical prophet Jonah fled God's command to preach in Nineveh and spent three days inside a great fish.
namesakes: Jonah Hill (actor, Superbad and Moneyball)

assoc.t: the biblical prophet swallowed by a great fish
a Jonah, sailors' term for a bringer of bad luck

e.etymology: The English spelling of Irish Méabh, from Middle Irish Medb, intoxicating. Medb is the legendary warrior queen of Connacht in the Irish epic Táin Bó Cúailnge.
namesakes: Queen Maeve of Connacht (warrior queen of Irish legend)
Maeve Millay (android madam in HBO's Westworld)
